extracted.intended_audience: peer reviewers for PLOS Medicine (research-active researchers asked to review manuscripts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for researchers acting as peer reviewers for PLOS Medicine, covering invitation acceptance, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, criteria for publication, how to write reviews, re-review expectations, and editorial decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting a review invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept an invitation only if you have the knowledge, time and objectivity necessary to provide an unbiased assessment of the research. In agreeing to complete a review, you also give permission to publish your review under a Creative Commons Attribution CC BY license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use links in the invitation email or the Editorial Manager system to accept/decline. Do not accept if you lack expertise, time, or objectivity. Be aware that accepting implies consent for the review to be published under CC BY.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review model / anonymity and signing
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS Medicine practices single-anonymized peer review by default (you will know the authors’ names; your name will not be shared). Reviewers can choose to sign their name to their review; if signed, authors and other reviewers will see the name. If authors publish their peer review history, signed names will accompany published comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to sign when submitting the review. Understand the implications for visibility if authors publish peer review history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews are portable: if authors transfer their manuscript to another PLOS journal your review will accompany it, and you may be asked to re-review by editors at another PLOS journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to have reviews considered by editors of other PLOS journals and potentially to perform re-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing interest is anything that interferes with or could be perceived as potentially interfering with a thorough and objective assessment of a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common examples include: a recent or current collaboration with any of the authors; direct competition or a history of scientific conflict with any of the authors; an opportunity to profit financially from the work. Do not accept a review assignment if you have a competing interest or cannot be objective. If unsure, contact the journal office for advice. If asked to complete the review despite a competing interest, declare it when you submit your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting collaborators who helped with the review
rubrics_metrics.description: If you had help completing the review you must share your collaborator’s name with the journal via email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include the collaborator’s name in the text of the review itself; inform the journal separately so the contribution is credited appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep manuscripts and correspondence confidential and do not share information about submissions with anyone else unless previously agreed with the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected not to make use of any material or take advantage of any information gained through the peer review process. See the PLOS Confidentiality Policy for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling manuscripts you previously reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: If you reviewed the article at another journal, consider the manuscript as a new submission unless instructed otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind it may have been revised since the prior review, and PLOS Medicine’s criteria for publication may differ. When submitting your review, inform the editor that you reviewed a previous version elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to complete a review
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to complete your review within 8 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need more time, email the journal as soon as possible to request an extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for publication (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to being conducted in accordance with ethical standards and scientifically valid, research published in PLOS Medicine should fulfill each of the following criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts must also comply with PLOS editorial and publishing policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research question importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The research question is an important one to the community of researchers in this general area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the question addressed matters to the field and relevant stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial advance and clear implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The results provide a substantial advance over existing knowledge, with clear implications for patient care, public policy, or clinical research agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novelty and the clarity/strength of implications for practice, policy, or future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest to clinicians and policymakers / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Published together with an Author Summary written for general readers, the article is of interest to clinicians and policymakers who are not specialists in this topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the findings are communicated in a way that will be useful and comprehensible to non-specialist clinicians and policymakers; assess the adequacy of the Author Summary if provided or required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the review (validity and actionable feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the review is to provide the editors with an expert opinion regarding the validity and quality of the manuscript and to supply authors with explicit feedback on how to improve their papers so that they will be acceptable for publication in PLOS Medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reviews that both advise editors on suitability and give authors clear, actionable suggestions for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify main claims and their significance
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the main claims of the paper and how significant are they for the discipline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the central claims and judge their importance to the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement in the literature and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims properly placed in the context of the previous literature? Have the authors treated the literature fairly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for omissions, selective citation, or misrepresentation of prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claims (data and analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the data and analyses fully support the claims? If not, what other evidence is required?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess appropriateness of analyses, robustness, and whether conclusions are warranted by the evidence; specify additional analyses or data needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods transparency and protocol deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS Medicine encourages authors to publish detailed methods as supporting information online. If a protocol is already provided, for example for a randomized controlled trial, are there any important deviations from it? If so, have the authors explained adequately why the deviations occurred?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend publishing methods as supporting information where appropriate; check that any deviations from protocols are justified and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether the paper is outstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this paper outstanding in its discipline? If yes, what makes it outstanding? If not, why not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear rationale for claims of exceptional importance or limitations preventing outstanding status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to relevant reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the study conform to any relevant guidelines such as CONSORT, MIAME, QUORUM, STROBE, and the Fort Lauderdale agreement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check adherence to appropriate reporting standards for the study design and data sharing expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Are details of the methodology sufficient to allow the experiments to be reproduced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify missing procedural details or materials needed for replication; recommend inclusion of supporting information where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Is any software created by the authors freely available?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request access to code or note if proprietary/closed software limits reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript organization and clarity for non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the manuscript well organized and written clearly enough to be accessible to non-specialists?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out major problems in structure, clarity, or jargon that impede understanding by clinicians or policymakers who are not topic specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confidential comments to editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Although confidential comments to the editors are respected, any remarks that might help to strengthen the paper should be directed to the authors themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve truly confidential material for the editor; otherwise, provide constructive feedback directly to authors so they can improve the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisions and re-review expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are often asked to evaluate revised manuscripts and the authors’ response to reviewer comments; reviewers should make themselves available for re-review and questions from the editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to assess whether revisions adequately address prior concerns and to provide timely re-reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and retention of reviewer reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Per PLOS’ Ethical Peer Review policy, journal editors do not delete reviewer reports. PLOS staff will not change reviewer comments intended for authors to read, except in cases where language is deemed inappropriate for professional communication, or if the comments contain confidential information or content that would pose a major risk if conveyed to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, PLOS will discuss wording changes with the reviewer; otherwise staff may make minimal edits. If feedback appears unreliable or misaligned with journal standards, staff or editors may advise authors that certain comments can be disregarded. Reviewers should be aware their reports will generally be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision process and handling conflicting reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors make the final decision on whether to publish each submission based on the reviewers’ comments, the PLOS Medicine criteria for publication, and their own assessment of the manuscript. If reviewers disagree fundamentally, editors may share reviews with reviewers and request additional comments; decisions are not necessarily made by majority rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that editors weigh reviews alongside other information and may seek further input to resolve conflicts; your recommendation is considered but not determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer credit and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Link your PLOS reviewer account to your ORCID or Publons record to receive credit for reviewing activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up syncing so reviewer activity is automatically posted to ORCID/Publons; this confirms you completed a review but does not publish the content of your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to get help and additional resources
rubrics_metrics.description: For more tips on peer review go to the Peer Review Center and sign up to the Peer Review Toolbox. If you have questions or need assistance submitting the review, contact plosmedicine@plos.org.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these resources for guidance on best practices, tools, and submission support.
